Debate was a public technology for comparing teachers and claims
Campā preserves unusually concrete evidence for a Brahman teacher and student circle
The Soṇadaṇḍa encounter shows learned communities sharing an urban audience
The samaṇa–brāhmaṇa landscape multiplied possible careers of knowledge
A debating hall is evidence for organised discussion, not automatically for a school building
Buddhist pedagogy used dialogue, repetition, lists and graduated explanation
The Saṅgha created a durable learning community through discipline and seniority
Collective recitation was both pedagogy and institutional quality control
Vaiśālī’s Second Council tradition reveals deliberation across a regional monastic network
Jain intellectual transmission depended on the fourfold community
Women were teachers, interlocutors, nuns and lay transmitters, but evidence remains uneven
Practical knowledge moved through apprenticeship even when texts remain silent
Patronage connected intellectual communities to households, markets and political power
Roads, ferries and cities were infrastructure for ideas as well as commodities
Later “university” models must not be projected onto early Videha, Vaiśālī or Campā
Conclusion: the eastern Ganga plain sustained plural intellectual communities through speech, mobility and institutions

social.title: Health, medicine and the body
social.part: Part Ii — Early Historic Society: Videha, Vajji And Anga
social.summary: Chapter argument. Health in early Mithilā–Videha, Vajji and Aṅga must be reconstructed from bodily vulnerability, care relationships, urban infrastructure, monastic regulation, specialist healing and the environmental conditions of dense settlement. The chapter does not project classical Āyurveda backward as a fully formed regional system, diagnose ancient populations from modern disease maps, or turn wells and…
sections: Health history begins with bodies under constraint, not with a timeless medical system
Five evidence streams must remain separate before synthesis
Archaeology is strongest for environments of health, weakest for named disease
Illness disrupted labour, ritual and mobility and therefore had economic effects
The professional healer is visible in literature before we can count physicians
Jīvaka’s fame should not be converted into proof of a standardised medical curriculum
Narrative surgery is evidence for an imagined therapeutic repertoire, not a modern operation report
The Buddhist Medicine Khandhaka preserves a practical pharmacology of monastic need
Food and medicine overlapped rather than belonging to sharply separate categories
Nursing was recognised as skilled moral labour inside the Saṅgha
The monastery could redistribute resources toward sickness without becoming a hospital
The body in Buddhist thought was both a site of suffering and an object of practical care
Jain asceticism placed a sharper ethical pressure on bodily treatment
Jain restraint and Buddhist therapeutic flexibility should not be turned into absolute opposites
Women’s health is visible only intermittently and must not be reconstructed from silence
Childhood and dependency enlarged the household economy of care
Occupational injury belonged to the ordinary health burden of an agrarian-craft society
Water management at Vaiśālī belongs to health history without becoming a sanitation myth
Campā’s ring-wells and brick drains show comparable urban pressures in Aṅga
Floodplain ecology created changing health risks that cannot be diagnosed retrospectively
Famine and epidemic are linked in the later Vaiśālī plague tradition, but the tradition is not a contemporary report
Aśoka’s second major rock edict marks a new scale of public language about medical welfare
Medicinal plants connected health to cultivation, trade and ecological knowledge
The market for treatment could combine fees, patronage, gifts and charity
Cleanliness, excreta and bodily waste were practical problems before germ theory
Classical Ayurveda is essential comparative evidence but its chronology must remain visible
Medical theory and medical practice need not have developed at the same speed
Health inequality followed differences in food, shelter, labour and social support
The strongest regional conclusions are infrastructural and institutional, not diagnostic
Conclusion: health was produced by households, specialists, institutions and environments together

social.title: From Vedic ritual landscapes to regional religious cultures
social.part: Part Iii — Religion, Ritual And Cultural Formation
social.summary: Chapter argument. Religious change in early Mithilā–Videha, Vajji and Aṅga was cumulative and plural. Vedic ritual traditions were extended eastward and transformed in the courts of Videha; Buddhist, Jain and other śramaṇa communities then became deeply embedded in the urban and political landscapes of Vaiśālī and Campā; and Mauryan and later monumentality made some sacred memories archaeologically durable. The…
sections: Religious history must begin with overlapping practices rather than modern labels
Four evidence streams have to be controlled before they are combined
The Śatapatha story of Videgha Māthava is a charter of ritual eastward movement
Sadānīrā was a symbolic threshold, but its exact modern identification remains debated
Videha did not remain a peripheral recipient of western ritual authority
Sacrificial patronage was an economic and political institution as well as a religious act
Janaka’s court is remembered as a place where ritual knowledge opened into philosophical inquiry
The presence of women in elite debate is significant but does not prove general gender equality
Archaeology cannot excavate “Vedic religion” from a pot type
The rise of śramaṇa movements belongs to the same changing eastern social world
“Greater Magadha” is a useful hypothesis when treated as a model rather than a fixed border
Vaiśālī became a meeting ground for political assembly and religious mobility
Mahāvīra’s Vaiśālī association is central to Jain regional memory
Jain asceticism reorganised the moral meaning of bodily action
Buddhist Vaiśālī traditions preserve several distinct institutional memories
Ambapālī’s gift illustrates how religious patronage could cross conventional status boundaries
Campā in Aṅga was a religious meeting-place embedded in a commercial city
Religious debate was a public technology for ranking persons and doctrines
The critique of sacrifice did not cause sacrifice to disappear
The archaeological record of early Buddhism begins later than many narrative settings
The Vaiśālī relic stūpa illustrates cumulative monumentality
Aśokan patronage marks a new documentary and monumental scale
Local cults and household religion remain the least visible part of the record
Sacred trees, groves and water bodies connected religion to landscape
Patronage linked religious authority to unequal distributions of wealth
Religious mobility depended on roads, ferries, seasons and political security
Language and oral transmission allowed religious communities to cross social boundaries
Religious identities became more durable as institutions acquired places, rules and memories
Long-term continuity should not be confused with unchanging tradition
Conclusion: the region became religiously important through interaction, not isolation

social.title: Buddhism in the social history of Vajji and Videha
social.part: Part Iii — Religion, Ritual And Cultural Formation
social.summary: Chapter argument. Buddhism became socially durable in Vajji and Videha through overlapping networks of mobility, patronage, political encounter, gendered participation, monastic regulation and sacred memory. Vesālī provides the densest combination of discourse, Vinaya and archaeological evidence; MN 91 provides unusually direct textual evidence for the Buddha’s itinerary in Videha and an encounter at Mithilā. The…
sections: Social history asks how Buddhism was embedded, not merely where the Buddha travelled
Four evidence streams must remain separate before synthesis
Vajji, Videha and Mithilā should not be flattened into modern administrative geography
The Brahmāyu Sutta gives unusually direct Buddhist evidence for Videha and Mithilā
Mithilā appears as a city of brahmins, householders, students and public religious reputation
Brahmāyu’s hospitality illustrates how lay conversion and material support could be joined
The Mithilā narrative is valuable precisely when its limits are stated
Vesālī was a recurrent Buddhist meeting-place rather than a single-event sacred site
Vesālī connected Buddhism with interregional diplomatic and intellectual traffic
The Vajjian political order forms part of the Buddhist social setting
Buddhist monastic order and Vajjian civic order are compared, but they are not identical institutions
Vesālī’s shrine landscape shows that Buddhism entered an already sacred city
Religious competition in Vesālī was social as well as doctrinal
Ambapālī is indispensable for the social history of Buddhist patronage
The contest between Ambapālī and the Licchavis dramatizes patronage as public status
Donation of a grove converted private or controlled property into institutional space
The alms economy linked monasteries to households every day
Buddhist mobility depended on roads, ferries, villages and remembered stopping-places
Seasonal residence changed the rhythm of relations between monks and local society
Vesālī became a foundational setting in Buddhist narratives about women’s ordination
The bhikkhunī tradition widens the social map beyond male monastic networks
Vinaya localization makes Vesālī a laboratory of institutional memory
Building, health and material rules reveal the practical density of monastic life at Vesālī
The Vesālī council tradition preserves memory of conflict inside an expanding Saṅgha
The dispute over money exposes the economic problem at the heart of renunciation
Relic claims turned Vajjian political identity into Buddhist civic memory
Archaeology at Vaiśālī demonstrates long Buddhist monumentality, not a one-to-one confirmation of texts
Aśokan commemoration transformed remembered places into an imperial Buddhist landscape
The strongest conclusions differ for Vesālī and Mithilā
Conclusion: Buddhism became regional through relationships, rules, spaces and memory

social.title: Jainism and the Vaishali–Videha landscape
social.part: Part Iii — Religion, Ritual And Cultural Formation
social.summary: Chapter argument. Jainism became socially embedded in the Vaiśālī–Videha landscape through disciplined ascetic mobility, repeated rainy-season residence, lay–monastic reciprocity, women’s and men’s participation, elite interaction and later sacred memory. The evidence is strongest when Jain canonical traditions, Buddhist external references, archaeology and later pilgrimage identifications are kept distinct before…
sections: A landscape history must distinguish remembered association from demonstrable institutional presence
Four evidence streams must be controlled separately before synthesis
The historical Mahāvīra is secure; the exact chronology and biography are not
Kuṇḍagrāma links Mahāvīra to the Vaiśālī–Videha zone, but its exact modern identification remains debated
The Jñātrika setting places renunciation inside an aristocratic and clan-based society
The Pārśva-following tradition suggests a pre-Mahāvīra ascetic inheritance, but not a fully documented institutional church
Vaiśālī’s political and urban environment made it a natural arena for competing renunciant communities
The Kalpa Sūtra preserves a powerful regional memory of repeated residence
Rainy-season residence changed the social mechanics of an itinerant ascetic movement
Vāṇijagrāma should be treated as a settlement name, not automatic proof of a merchant-dominated Jain economy
Mithilā belongs to Jain remembered geography independently of later medieval scholastic fame
Campā and Pṛṣṭhacampā extend the Jain social horizon eastward into Aṅga
Buddhist references provide an external control on Jain presence at Vesālī
The Sīha narrative reveals competition over prestige, patronage and ethical reputation
Inter-sectarian debate sharpened identities without creating sealed communities
Jain ascetic mobility transformed ordinary landscapes into ethical terrain
Ahiṃsā was a demanding discipline before it became a general emblem of Jain identity
Non-possession increased rather than eliminated the importance of lay support
The fourfold community made gender and household status part of Jain institutional design
Women’s renunciation is integral to the regional story, even where biographies are hagiographic
Lay vows adapted ascetic ethics to household life without making householders miniature monks
Early Jain social history should not be rewritten through the stereotype of the later merchant community
Political kinship traditions are evidence of how Jains remembered patronage, not transparent diplomatic archives
Jain ethics challenged status at the level of liberation while communities still operated inside stratified society
Canonical language records transmission history, not a verbatim transcript of Mahāvīra’s speech
Vaiśālī’s archaeology supplies the urban setting but does not yet provide a secure early Jain institutional footprint
Later pilgrimage landscapes preserve memory while also relocating and monumentalising it
Jainism belongs to the wider eastern Gangetic śramaṇa world, but no single cultural boundary explains everything
The evidence is strongest for networks and repeated association, weaker for population size and exclusive territory
Conclusion: Jainism became regional through disciplined movement, repeated residence, lay support and remembered place

social.title: Śaiva, Śākta and Vaiṣṇava transformations
social.part: Part Iii — Religion, Ritual And Cultural Formation
social.summary: Chapter argument. Between the late ancient and early medieval centuries, Śaiva, Śākta and Vaiṣṇava traditions became increasingly visible in Mithila, Vajji and Aṅga through image installation, temples, ritual specialists, patronage, sacred water and pilgrimage. The transformation was cumulative rather than a single conversion: Buddhist, Jain, Vedic, household and local practices continued within a poly-religious…
sections: Transformation is a historical process, not a switch from one religion to another
Four evidence streams must be kept separate before they are combined
The Gupta and post-Gupta centuries intensified iconic and temple-centred worship
Śaivism was not one organisation but a family of ritual and theological formations
Śaiva institutions connected renunciation, temple ritual and political patronage
The liṅga is a ritual object whose history cannot be reduced to a modern symbol
Śākta history requires distinguishing goddess worship from later formal Śākta systems
The Devīmāhātmya helped articulate a goddess who could absorb multiple divine powers
Goddess images reveal public materialisation, not simply private belief
Śākta and Śaiva traditions often intersected rather than occupying separate worlds
Vaiṣṇava transformation joined older Viṣṇu traditions to image, temple and avatāra devotion
Aṅga’s Mandar Hill provides a rare inscriptional anchor for regional Vaiṣṇava patronage
Sacred water, temple patronage and kingship formed a linked social technology
Pāla political history does not equal a Buddhist monopoly on religious life
Art-historical style can connect a sculpture to a region and period, but not reconstruct its whole institution
Mithila’s surviving medieval sculptures show plurality rather than a single sectarian landscape
Recent recoveries from ponds and fields demonstrate both archaeological richness and loss of context
Vaiṣṇava images in Bihar demonstrate sophisticated iconographic production and patronage
Image installation created durable obligations of care
Temple growth changed the spatial organisation of religious life
Sectarian texts and actual village practice operated at different levels
Tantric transformations linked body, mantra, deity and power in new ritual configurations
Śākta power should not be reduced to a story of “tribal absorption”
Vaiṣṇava avatāra theology allowed regional landscapes to connect with pan-Indian narratives
Religious patronage was not mechanically determined by dynastic identity
Gender appears in patronage, goddess theology and ritual participation in different ways
Religious specialists became mediators between textual systems and local society
Poly-religiosity is a better model for early medieval Bihar than a zero-sum contest
The evidence is strongest for material and institutional visibility, weaker for population percentages
Conclusion: Śaiva, Śākta and Vaiṣṇava traditions transformed the region by building durable institutions into an already plural landscape

social.title: Sacred geography
social.part: Part Iii — Religion, Ritual And Cultural Formation
social.summary: Chapter argument. Sacred geography in Mithila, Vajji and Aṅga was produced cumulatively through remembered narratives, repeated movement, water and route infrastructure, monuments, patronage and later pilgrimage. The chapter separates textual, archaeological, epigraphic and later devotional evidence so that modern holy places are not projected backward as unchanged ancient sites. It then reconstructs how rivers,…
sections: Sacred geography is made through historical practice, not discovered as a timeless map
Four evidence streams must be dated separately before a sacred landscape is reconstructed
The Indian category of tīrtha links crossing, place and social movement
The Ganga formed the southern horizon of Mithila and a major east–west religious corridor
The Sadānīrā/Gandak memory shows how a river could become a cultural boundary in narrative
The Kosi warns against assuming that sacred landscapes remain physically fixed
Groves were social spaces where mobility could become repeated sacred association
Ponds and tanks joined ritual efficacy to water management
Campā’s Gaggarā lotus pond is a strong example of a named water-place in textual sacred geography
Vaiśālī became sacred through the accumulation of several religious maps rather than one exclusive tradition
Relic stupas and pillars turned memory into durable spatial markers
Jain sacred geography relied heavily on movement, seasonal residence and remembered biography
Mithilā’s sacred prestige began in more than one textual tradition
Janakpur demonstrates the historical re-creation of a sacred city
Ramayana localisation connected Mithila to a transregional narrative world
Janakpur’s ponds and parikrama show how a sacred city is organised through movement
Mandar Hill is one of Aṅga’s clearest examples of a natural feature becoming a multi-layered sacred centre
The Mandar tank inscription demonstrates how patronage could bind deity, water and royal memory
Mandar’s later plurality illustrates how sacred places can be shared without becoming religiously identical
Vikramaśīla transformed the Aṅga–Bhagalpur Ganga corridor into a major monastic-intellectual sacred node
Pilgrimage routes were social corridors, not lines drawn independently of roads and seasons
Pilgrimage created recurring demand for hospitality, food and ritual services
Artisans helped convert remembered places into visible sacred landscapes
Women appear in sacred geography as patrons, renouncers, pilgrims and remembered figures
Rulers used sacred landscapes to make authority visible, but religious patronage was not simple propaganda
Poly-religious landscapes are better understood through shared infrastructure and differentiated meaning
Evidence is strongest for named associations and material investment, weaker for exact ancient localisation and uninterrupted continuity
Conclusion: sacred geography was a cumulative social technology of memory, movement and materialisation

social.title: Festivals and calendrical culture
social.part: Part Iii — Religion, Ritual And Cultural Formation
social.summary: Chapter argument. Calendrical culture in Mithila, Vajji and Aṅga developed through the interaction of lunar and solar reckoning, seasonal ecology, monastic discipline, specialist astronomy, household ritual and regional festival practice. The chapter distinguishes durable calendrical structures from the much more difficult question of the antiquity of individual festivals, and treats the ritual year as a social…
sections: Calendars are social infrastructure, not merely systems for naming dates
Four evidence streams must be kept separate before the ritual year is reconstructed
Early Vedic ritual already required coordination of lunar, solar and seasonal time
The lunar fortnight made recurring observance easy to organise across mobile communities
Lunisolar coordination required correction because lunar months do not equal the solar year
The Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa represents a major stage in the formalisation of ritual astronomy, but its date is debated
Seasons were not merely astronomical divisions; they were experienced through monsoon ecology
Buddhist uposatha institutionalised lunar observance as a recurring communal discipline
The rains residence converted climate into an institutional season
Jain rainy-season discipline created a parallel but distinct temporal institution
Calendrical regularity allowed institutions to plan labour, food and hospitality
Dated inscriptions reveal another calendrical world: the time of rulers, donations and legal memory
The Lakṣmaṇa Sena era shows that regional year-counting could coexist with wider Indian systems
Pañcāṅga specialists mediated between astronomical computation and household decisions
Muhūrta culture distributed expertise unevenly across society
Life-cycle rites occupied a different temporal logic from annual festivals
Women’s vratas demonstrate that calendrical culture also organised gendered religious agency
Sāmā-Cakevā provides unusually rich ethnographic evidence for a women-centred Maithil festival cycle
Madhushrāvaṇī connects monsoon time, marriage and women’s narrative-ritual practice
Chhath demonstrates the power of a solar-facing rite embedded within a lunar festival calendar
Moon-oriented and regional rites show that the same celestial body can support highly local meanings
Festival cycles often cluster at seasonal transitions rather than being evenly distributed through the year
Agricultural season and ritual season intersect, but one cannot be reduced to the other
Festival time can activate sacred geography by turning ordinary routes and water places into temporary centres
Calendrical participation varies by caste, sect, gender, age and household tradition
The India–Nepal border did not divide the Maithil ritual year into two sealed systems
Printed almanacs changed the circulation of calendrical authority without eliminating oral expertise
Modern state holidays, media and migration have created new layers of calendrical culture
Conclusion: calendrical culture repeatedly turns cosmic cycles into social coordination

social.title: Death, ancestors and life-cycle rites
social.part: Part Iii — Religion, Ritual And Cultural Formation
social.summary: Chapter argument. Life-cycle rites do not simply preserve an unchanged religious system from antiquity to the present. They convert biological events—conception, birth, maturation, marriage, ageing and death—into socially recognised transitions, and their forms change with household structure, inheritance, gender, ritual authority, religious affiliation and historical period. Mortuary practice is especially…
sections: Life-cycle rites transform biological events into social transitions
Six evidence problems make mortuary history unusually difficult
The classical list of saṃskāras is itself a historical construction
Rigvedic funerary hymns reveal both cremation and an ancestor-oriented imagination
The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa makes the mortuary landscape itself part of ritual order
Fire transformed the corpse while also reorganising relations among the living
Bone collection and memorialisation show that cremation does not erase materiality
Mourning and impurity regulate the temporary disorder produced by death
Ancestors convert genealogy into a continuing moral and ritual relationship
Śrāddha became a major technology for incorporating the dead among the ancestors
Birth rites demonstrate that life-cycle ritual begins by making a new person socially legible
Naming, first feeding and hair rites organise childhood as a sequence rather than an undifferentiated stage
Initiation made education, ritual entitlement and male status intersect
Marriage is both a life-cycle rite and a reorganisation of kinship, property and residence
Women’s positions in life-cycle ritual cannot be reconstructed from male prescriptions alone
Death is also a property event because rights and obligations must outlive the deceased
Ritual specialists turn life-cycle knowledge into a form of service and authority
Buddhist mortuary practice shifted emphasis without eliminating social ritual around death
The Mahāparinibbāna tradition makes cremation, political claim and relic division one connected social drama
The Licchavi claim to the Buddha’s relics gave Vaiśālī a mortuary memory of exceptional durability
The excavated Vaiśālī relic stupa gives material evidence independent of the literary narrative
Relic monuments turn the dead into institutions that require labour, patronage and repeated visitation
Buddhist merit practices broadened remembrance beyond biological descent
Jain traditions made disciplined dying a distinctive ascetic problem, not a general household funeral rule
Jain household mortuary practice is less visible in early regional evidence than Jain ascetic ideals
Archaeology rarely permits the religion or community of an ordinary cremation to be identified confidently
Rivers and water connect mortuary practice to ecology, mobility and sacred geography
Later Mithila developed dense life-cycle ritual systems, but their antiquity must be demonstrated rather than presumed
Continuity is most persuasive at the level of recurring social problems, not identical ritual scripts
Conclusion: death and life-cycle rites reveal how society reproduces itself across generations
